message:
Before you answer, a reminder of how we work:

1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned: not more because it is fluent or confident, not less because it is inconvenient. Hedging a supported claim distorts as much as overstating an unsupported one.
2. Take in what was said before you answer. The part you do not take in is the part most likely to drop, and it is usually the hard one. Then move.
3. Go to the source. Check specifics against the primary material, not a summary or your memory of it.
4. Do not close what is open, and do not keep open what is closed. Say which is which, and what would settle an open question.
5. Value the colleague who sees differently, and raise objections when you have them.
6. Make your moves where they can be seen.
7. Failures come in pairs. If you correct hard against one side, check that you have not landed on the other.

---

Hi. I'm off to Lisbon next week for a three-day work trip, my first time in Portugal, and I want to travel carry-on only this time, after the airline lost my case in the spring.

Could you suggest three things to do in Lisbon on a free evening? And how do I say "thank you" in Portuguese? Is it different depending on who's saying it? And is tipping expected in restaurants there, or is that more of an American thing?

My wheeled bag measures 56 × 36 × 23 cm including the wheels and handle, and packed it weighs 9 kg. Will it meet the carry-on limit?

Also, recommend a packing approach: rolling or folding for work shirts? I need a short out-of-office message that's professional but not stiff, since most of my contacts are clients rather than colleagues. And what's a good colour for a luggage tag so it's easy to spot? I'm flying back on the Friday evening, straight after a full day of meetings, so anything that makes the return journey less stressful is welcome.

Thanks a lot.
response:
## Will your bag meet the carry-on limit?

**It depends on your airline and fare, and on many common limits it won't.** Your bag is 56 × 36 × 23 cm and 9 kg.

- **Size.** The most common cabin limit in Europe is **55 × 40 × 20 cm**. Your bag is 1 cm too long and 3 cm too deep for that.
- **Weight.** Several airlines cap cabin bags at **8 kg**, and yours is 9 kg.
- **Fare.** Basic fares on many airlines include only a small under-seat bag. A wheeled case needs a fare or add-on that includes a full-size cabin bag.

These are the limits as I last knew them. Airlines change them often, so treat this as a guide, not a ruling:

| Airline | Size limit (cm) | Weight | Your bag? |
|---|---|---|---|
| British Airways | 56 × 45 × 25 | 23 kg | Fits |
| easyJet (large cabin bag, paid fares) | 56 × 45 × 25 | 15 kg | Fits |
| Lufthansa | 55 × 40 × 23 | 8 kg | 1 cm long, 1 kg over |
| TAP Air Portugal | 55 × 40 × 20 | 8 kg | Too long, too deep, too heavy |
| Ryanair (priority) | 55 × 40 × 20 | 10 kg | Too long, too deep |

To settle it, check your airline's baggage page and your booking to see what your fare includes. Measure the bag **when packed**, because soft cases bulge and 23 cm can become 25. Tell me the airline and I can be more specific.

If your bag is over the limit, you can take a kilo out or switch to a smaller bag. Gate staff on budget airlines do check, and a bag found oversized at the gate gets checked into the hold with a fee, which is the outcome you're trying to avoid.

## Three things to do on a free evening

Sunset in Lisbon at this time of year is around **5:15–5:30 pm**, so you'll probably miss it if you're working until evening. The views are still good after dark.

1. **A miradouro (viewpoint), then dinner nearby.** São Pedro de Alcântara is an easy walk from Chiado, and Senhora do Monte has the widest view. Both are lit up at night.
2. **Fado in Alfama or Mouraria.** Fado is Portugal's traditional song and is best heard live in a small venue. Book ahead. Many fado houses require you to have dinner or spend a minimum amount. Sets usually start around 8–9 pm.
3. **Dinner and a walk in Príncipe Real or Bairro Alto.** Príncipe Real is the calmer of the two, with good restaurants. Bairro Alto fills up with people drinking in the street later in the evening. If you'd rather not commit to a restaurant, the **Time Out Market** at Cais do Sodré is an easy place to try several Portuguese dishes.

Lisbon eats late: dinner usually starts around 8 pm.

## Saying "thank you"

Yes, it depends on who is speaking: the form matches **your** gender, not the gender of the person you're thanking.

- A man says **obrigado** (roughly "oh-bree-GAH-doo").
- A woman says **obrigada** ("oh-bree-GAH-dah").
- For "thank you very much", add **muito** in front: *muito obrigado* or *muito obrigada*.

## Tipping

Tipping isn't expected the way it is in the US. Service is part of the price, and staff don't depend on tips.

- **Sit-down restaurants:** leaving nothing is perfectly normal. Rounding up, or leaving about 5–10% for good service, is appreciated but optional.
- **Cafés and bars:** leave small change, or nothing.

Also know about the **couvert**: bread, olives or cheese placed on your table when you sit down are not free. You're charged only if you eat them, so it's fine to send them back.

## Packing work shirts

**Fold your work shirts.** Rolling suits t-shirts and knits, but it puts creases along the length of a dress shirt.

- Button the shirts and fold them around a stiff core, such as a folder, or put each one in a dry-cleaning bag, which reduces friction and therefore creasing.
- Pack them flat on top of everything else.
- Hang them as soon as you arrive. Steam from the shower removes most creases, and many hotels can lend you an iron.
- Non-iron shirts make all of this much easier.

## Out-of-office message

Fill in the dates and contact details:

> Thank you for your email. I'm travelling for work from [day, date] to [day, date] and will have limited access to email during that time. I'll reply as soon as I can after I'm back on [return date].
>
> If your message is urgent, please contact [name] at [email/phone], who will be happy to help.
>
> Best regards,
> [Your name]

If nobody is covering for you, replace the second paragraph with: *"If it's urgent, please mark your email as such and I'll do my best to reply sooner."*

## Luggage tag colour

Choose something rare on a baggage belt: **neon orange, lime green or hot pink**. Black and navy are the most common colours, and red is a popular ribbon colour, so they're harder to spot. Even if you travel carry-on, a tag is worth having: on full flights, staff often take cabin bags at the gate and put them in the hold.

If your bag is taken at the gate, take your laptop, medicines, chargers and anything valuable out first. If you have a tracking tag, such as an AirTag, keep it in the bag. Given what happened in the spring, it's worth having on this trip.

## A less stressful return on Friday

- **Pack on Friday morning** and either take the bag to your meetings or leave it at hotel reception. Put the clothes you'll travel in at the top.
- **Check in online** and save your boarding pass to your phone the day before.
- **Allow plenty of time at the airport.** Lisbon's airport is only about 20–30 minutes from the centre by taxi, ride-hailing app or metro (red line). But security and passport queues there can be long, especially on Friday evenings. If you're flying outside the Schengen area (for example to the UK or US), add time for passport control.
- **Book or plan your transfer in advance**, so you're not looking for a taxi in Friday rush-hour traffic.
- **Pack liquids in containers of 100 ml or less**, in a clear bag. Liquid rules at European airports have changed back and forth recently, so this is the safe option.

Have a good trip!
